The brand palette: storm-ocean steel on a cool, mist-grey base (the redesign, workshop 5 round 9).

## Rules that govern every colour here, MEASURED rather than a matter of taste

Every pair a component paints is declared and measured against WCAG 2.2 AA in
`__tests__/redesignContrast.test.ts` (4.5:1 for text, SC 1.4.3; 3:1 for large text, component edges and graphics,
SC 1.4.11), in both themes; the values are pinned to the design session's sources in `__tests__/redesignPin.test.ts`.
The ratios are NOT restated here: a number in a comment is a second copy that goes stale when a tier moves.

Three rules the tests cannot state for you:

 1. **A tier is a FILL or it is TEXT, and a tier that is both has a darker text sibling.** `error` fills a
    destructive control under a light label and `error-dark` is the red a reader reads; `warning` is the caution
    fill and `warning-dark` its text. `steel` is both a fill and, on the cool canvas, text and an edge.
 2. **Steel is an ACCENT, never a large fill.** A filled `action` is for buttons, the floating action button, the
    selected segment, checked boxes and the current step number. A large selected area (a row, a tile, a
    panel) uses `selectedFill`, never `action`.
 3. **`mist` is a hairline tone, never text**, and an ALPHA-tinted text colour is not a text colour: the token
    passes while the rendered pixel does not. A dimmed label uses the opaque muted role.

## Names

`steel`, `steel-light` and `fog` were `seafoam`, `seafoam-light` and `sand` before the redesign; a key that still
said teal or sand would mislead the next reader, so they were renamed with every consumer (`bg-steel`,
`from-steel`, `palette['steel-light']` ...). `honey` (the amber star) and `premium` (the PRO tan) are gone: the
redesign made each a copy of another entry (`charcoal`, `slate`), and a duplicate that keeps a stale name is a trap.
`__tests__/redesignRetired.test.ts` fails if a retired value comes back.

Web spacing scale — `rem` strings derived from the single numeric source (`scale.spacing`, px ÷16),
with the unitless `0`. `space` and `size` share the same ramp (Tamagui parity on the mobile side).

Web corner radii — `rem` derived from the single numeric source (`scale.radius`, px ÷16). The `full`
pill sentinel is emitted as `px` (a `rem` pill would scale with the root font, which we don't want).

Web elevation — CSS `box-shadow` strings composed from the single numeric source (`scale.elevation`).
`glow` is the steel focus halo; the rest are soft drop shadows.
Web font families — the shared stacks from the single source.

Web font sizes — `rem` derived from the single numeric source (`scale.fontSize`, px ÷16). Keys stay in
the web's kebab-case (`display-xl` …) convention; the ramp order is largest → smallest.
Web font weights — the numeric weights from the single source, as CSS `font-weight` strings.

The brand gradients. `brand` is the steel → ocean-dark CTA ramp (identical to the web Button's
`from-steel to-ocean-dark`); `hero` is the flat canvas wash that paints the home/recipes/auth hero surfaces.

The React Native projection of the design scale. `spacing`/`radius`/`fontSize` are pixel numbers,
`lineHeight` is the px leading for each allowed size, `fontWeight` are numeric weights, and `elevation` are RN shadow objects.

Type is projected as `fontFace` — the REGISTERED face names — and NOT as the web `fontFamily` stacks:
React Native resolves `fontFamily` to one registered face, so handing it a stack silently renders the
system font. Withholding the stack here is what makes that bug unrepresentable on native (guarded by
`__tests__/nativeFontFace.test.ts`).

Spacing scale in pixels on a 4px base (step index → px). Web emits `rem` (÷16, unitless `0`);
native and Tamagui use the pixel number directly.

Corner radii in pixels. `full` is a pill sentinel — web emits it as `px` (not `rem`); Tamagui maps
it to its highest numeric radius step.

The named type ramp — font size in pixels, largest to smallest. Web emits `rem` under kebab-case keys
(`display-md` …); native uses the pixel number. Every value is one of 14, 16, 18 or 28 (the owner's type-scale
ruling, pinned by `__tests__/typeScale.test.ts`); several names share a size because a name says what a step is
for, and the rule says how many sizes there are. Nothing above 28: the 48 and 36 steps are retired.
Numeric font weights (web stringifies them; native/Tamagui keep the `'400'`-style string form).

Line height in px for each allowed font size (owner ruling 2026-10-25: line heights are whole px on a 4 px grid).
A pixel value is the source of truth: native uses it as is, and web writes it as the unitless `calc(px / size)`.
18 is 24 for a heading or figure; reading text sets itself at 28 (`typeRole.readingBody`).

Elevation specs, each a stack of one or two shadow layers (the redesign's cool, soft shadows). Web composes a CSS
`box-shadow` from EVERY layer (spread omitted when 0); native has one shadow per view, so it takes the LAST layer,
the diffuse one that carries the depth. `glow` is the focus halo: a 3 px ring, no blur.

The `glow` colour is DERIVED from `palette.steel` ({@link rgbTriplet}), so the halo cannot drift from the button
it rings.

Named MEDIA-BOX heights in pixels — the geometry of a lead image surface, which is a design decision
(how much of a screen the cover claims) rather than a spacing step, so it is named rather than derived
from the 4px ramp.

`hero` is the recipe-detail cover box: the mockup's `h-64` phone value (`screenRecipeDetail`).
`heroPlaceholder` is the deliberately COMPACT band the no-cover fallback paints on a phone — a full-height
empty gradient would claim most of a phone's first screen and push the title below the fold. Web keeps the
full box on both states because a desktop hero has the room; see `RecipeHero.native.tsx` for the rationale.

Font families as CSS font-stack strings — **web only** (`--font-*`). A stack is meaningless to React
Native, whose `fontFamily` resolves exactly one REGISTERED face; native display type selects a face from
{@link displayFontFace} instead (and `nativeTokens` deliberately exposes no stack at all).

The REGISTERED native faces of the display family, keyed by the {@link fontWeight} step each one paints.

React Native resolves `fontFamily` to a single registered face name; handed the CSS stack above it falls
back to the system face **silently** — brand type that never renders and never errors. These are the
faces the apps load at start-up (`@expo-google-fonts/manrope`), and they are single-sourced here
so no consumer re-types a face-name literal. Their shape is asserted against {@link fontFamily}.display
and {@link fontWeight} in the token tests, so renaming the family or moving a weight step cannot leave a
stale name pointing at a font nobody loads.
